tier_reason: Peer-reviewed OSDI '20 paper (osdi20-fried.pdf) states every claimed figure in the text: 11,000x and 580 ms vs 52 us against Parties*, 235x/6x/75% for Linux/Shenango, and 43x, 5x and 560k vs 285k for KSCHED vs Linux syscalls. It is not A because neither the paper nor the artifact gives a CPU model ('Xeon Broadwell') or compiler/flags, and the artifact has no driver for the baseline runs. I did not apply the >50x cap: the 11,000x is a GC-window tail-latency result explained by Parties' 500 ms adjustment interval, not a compiler-sensitive microbenchmark.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Vs Parties* (memcached + swaptions-GC): 99.9% latency 11,000x lower during GC cycles ('reducing tail latency from 580 ms to 52 us'), and Parties* BE throughput averaged 5% less than Caladan's. Vs Linux and Shenango (constant stream-DRAM interference, Fig. 4): their tail latency rose 'up to 235x and 6x higher than without interference' and Shenango's throughput fell 75%. Caladan (and Parties*) kept similar tail latency with and without interference and achieved 'much higher throughput than Linux and Shenango' (graph only, no exact numbers). KSCHED vs a variant using Linux syscalls (sched_setaffinity/tgkill/eventfd): the Linux variant needs 43x more scheduling work and 5x the scheduling latency when moving 22 tasks, and bottlenecks at ~285,000 core reallocations/s vs Caladan's peak of 560,000 (at 0.65 MRPS).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The current repo build (build/shared.mk) uses CC ?= gcc (CONFIG_CLANG=y switches to clang), -std=gnu11 for C and -std=gnu++20 for C++, and -O3 -DNDEBUG; CONFIG_OPTIMIZE=y adds -march=native -flto=auto -ffat-lto-objects -ffast-math. These are today's flags, not the 2020 evaluation build.
corrections.caveats: The 11,000x figure is against the authors' own reimplementation of Parties, which they gave kernel-bypass networking and hyperthreads (hence 'Parties*'). It is a peak-window value taken only during GC cycles (580 ms vs 52 us), not a steady-state average; the separate 500,000x figure is convergence speed compared with Parties' published typical speed. The Linux and Shenango comparison exists only as a graph (Fig. 4): the 235x and 6x ratios compare those systems with and without interference, not with Caladan, and Caladan's throughput lead over Linux comes mostly from kernel-bypass networking. The Linux baseline also ran a different kernel (5.4.0 vs modified 5.2.0). Neither Parties* nor Linux is a listed event-loops-io baseline (libuv/libevent/epoll/io_uring). IX and Arachne appear in related work only and were not measured. No compiler or flags are given, and the CPU is named only as 'Xeon Broadwell'; security mitigations were disabled. The artifact repo (github.com/shenango/caladan-all, which has no license file) has a paper_experiments.py that drives only Caladan configurations (figure 7, 8, 9b ksched-vs-pinned, 9c and the memcached timeseries). Its helper code has partial linux/shenango configurations and a memcached-linux submodule, but there is no driver for the Parties*, Linux/Shenango (Fig. 4) or Linux-syscall-variant comparisons. These are 2020 numbers, and the code has changed a lot since then (current kernels 5.15/6.8, directpath, DPDK PMDs).

notes: All numbers and hardware details match the OSDI '20 PDF. Metadata checked via GitHub GraphQL (REST was rate-limited): Apache-2.0, 200 stars, 78 forks, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-05-10, so active. I set baseline_in_list to false to match wave 5 precedent (Shenango, Demikernel and FlexTOE with Linux-kernel baselines are false).

tier_reason: arXiv 2502.09281v1 is a first-party, pre-review preprint. Its text and figures give every claimed number: 2.6x/4.2x/7.4x (Fig. 10: 70/134/365 us vs 27/32/49 us), FASTER 700K vs 210K RPS with p99 50 vs 250 us, and Raft p50 185 vs 282 us and p99 625 vs 1000 us. It is not A because the CPU model and compiler are not stated and the FASTER and Raft benchmark code is not public. The peer-reviewed ASPLOS '26 text could not be read, so tier B cannot be confirmed.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 162 stars, 33 forks. eRPC's README opens with a Dec 2023 news line telling users to check out Machnet.
corrections.caveats: The numbers come from arXiv v1 (Feb 2025, 'Fast Userspace Networking for the Rest of Us', where the figures still label the system 'CNet'). The arXiv API shows no later version as of 2026-09-26. That is a pre-review, first-party version. The peer-reviewed paper is 'Enabling Fast Networking in the Public Cloud', ASPLOS '26, pp. 679-696, DOI 10.1145/3779212.3790158, with a changed author list. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex mark it Gold OA (CC-BY), and the Machnet docs site links it, but dl.acm.org returned 403 and the PoliMi IRIS record has no file, so the final numbers are unverified. That is why this is tier C; it would be B if the ASPLOS text keeps these comparisons. The Linux baseline is kernel TCP via sockperf, which is not a listed websocket-grpc-rpc baseline (gRPC/uWebSockets/Thrift). That baseline is untuned: Nagle is off, but busy-polling sockets, isolcpus and IRQ steering are not used (the paper omits isolcpus and interrupt steering for all stacks), while Machnet dedicates a polling core. Against eRPC (a known-list project, not a category baseline) Machnet is slower: its median and p99 are within 10% of eRPC and p99.9 within 23%, and its 27 us median is 2 us higher. gRPC was not measured; the paper only asserts that libraries on top of Linux TCP such as gRPC would be slower. Only one Azure region was used, and the paper says cross-cloud numbers are not comparable. The paper's Raft text says '37% lower median p99', and Fig. 8 shows p99 625 vs 1000 us. On the repo side, the benchmark apps in the tree are src/apps/msg_gen, src/apps/rocksdb_server (not in the paper) and bindings/go/msg_gen; the FASTER server and Raft port are not in the tree, and the Linux side used sockperf. The README headline (750K 1KB RPCs/s at 61 us P99.9) has no baseline.

notes: Every claimed number matches arXiv v1. I tried for a readable ASPLOS '26 copy: arXiv API (v1 only), ACM PDF (403), OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, PoliMi IRIS (no file), Antichi's and Kaffes's pages and the Machnet docs site (links only to ACM). None had the full text, so tier stays C. Metadata checked via GitHub GraphQL: MIT, 162 stars, 33 forks, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-04-21, so active.
